title: Doppler effect
examples: What happens to the pitch of a siren as it moves away from me?
How does the speed of the source affect the observed frequency?
Can the Doppler effect be seen with light waves too?

explain.say: Today we explore the Doppler effect for waves. This effect describes the change in wave frequency. This change happens when the source or observer is moving. We will look at how motion affects what we hear.

items: Source stationary, Observer stationary: Frequency observed equals source frequen
Source moving towards observer: Observed frequency increases (higher pitch).
Source moving away from observer: Observed frequency decreases (lower pitch).

explain.say: Next we look at the moving source scenario. If the source of sound moves towards you, the waves bunch up. This bunching up makes the frequency appear higher to you. Think about an ambulance siren approaching.
Now consider the source moving away from you. As the source moves away, the waves spread out more. This spreading out lowers the observed frequency. This is why the pitch drops as it passes.

The Doppler effect also applies when the observer moves. If you move towards a stationary source, you hear a higher frequency. This is because you are encountering wave crests faster. Imagine standing near a passing train.
A crucial link exists between the Doppler effect and light. When light sources move away from Earth, their light waves stretch. This stretching is called redshift, and it is seen in the spectrum.

In everyday life, the Doppler effect helps us measure speed. Police radar guns use this effect to measure the speed of vehicles. They detect the frequency shift of the reflected radio waves. This allows them to calculate the speed accurately.

draw.text: Radar guns measure speed via frequency shift

faq.q: Does the Doppler effect only work for sound waves?
faq.a: No, the Doppler effect applies to all types of waves, including light waves. The change in frequency is what is measured regardless of the wave type. You can see this effect with light from stars.
asks: Does it only happen with sound?
Is it only for audible waves?

faq.q: What is the difference between redshift and blueshift?
faq.a: Redshift means the frequency is lowered, indicating the source is moving away from us. Blueshift means the frequency is increased, indicating the source is moving towards us. This relates directly to the Doppler effect.
asks: What does redshift mean for light?
How do I know if something is moving away?

faq.q: Does the speed of the source or observer matter more?
faq.a: Both the speed of the source and the speed of the observer affect the final observed frequency. The formula accounts for both relative motions. Neither one can be ignored when calculating the shift.
asks: Do I use both speeds in the calculation?

faq.q: If I am stationary, how do I measure the speed of a moving source?
faq.a: You measure the change in frequency over time. The greater the measured frequency shift, the faster the source is moving. This is the principle behind radar guns.
asks: How do I find speed from frequency?
What does a large shift mean?

faq.q: Is the Doppler effect always noticeable?
faq.a: It is most noticeable with sound waves because our ears are designed to perceive pitch changes. However, the effect is mathematically present for all waves.
asks: Can I hear this effect easily?

facts: The Doppler effect describes the perceived change in frequency. This change occurs due to relative motion between source and observer. For light waves, the stretching of light is called redshift. The effect is measurable for sound waves and electromagnetic waves.
When a source moves towards an observer, the perceived frequency increases. When it moves away, the perceived frequency decreases.
Redshift in light indicates that the light source is moving away from the observer. Blueshift indicates movement towards the observer.

quiz.say: A siren approaches a stationary person. The observed pitch sounds higher than normal. This demonstrates which effect?
quiz.why: When the source moves toward you, the waves are compressed, making the frequency higher.

wrong.0: This describes waves adding up, but ignores the effect of the source's speed.
wrong.2: This is a general term for bouncing waves, not specifically related to source motion.
wrong.3: This law relates intensity to distance, not the frequency shift due to motion.

quiz.say: Astronomers observe a galaxy whose light has a redshift. What does this imply about the galaxy's movement?

options.show: The light source is changing color.
options.say: The light source is changing color.

options.show: The galaxy is moving away from Earth.
options.say: The galaxy is moving away from Earth.

options.show: The galaxy is moving towards Earth.
options.say: The galaxy is moving towards Earth.

quiz.why: Redshift means the light waves are stretched, which happens when the source moves away from the observer.

wrong.0: While color changes, the physical cause here is the Doppler shift due to velocity.
wrong.2: A stationary source would show no significant redshift or blueshift.
wrong.3: Movement towards Earth causes a blueshift, not a redshift.

quiz.say: If an observer moves directly towards a stationary sound source, the perceived frequency will:
quiz.why: Moving towards the source allows the observer to encounter wave crests more frequently, increasing perceived frequency.

wrong.1: Decreasing frequency happens only when moving away from the source.
wrong.2: The observer's motion directly influences the rate of wave reception.
wrong.3: The frequency only becomes zero if the source is infinitely far away.
